newsitem.title: CHINA: HK to play role in China-Taiwan ties -- analysts.
newsitem.headline: HK to play role in China-Taiwan ties -- analysts.

text.p: Stalemated China-Taiwan relations will get a nudge from Hong Kong's handover but Beijing will play a waiting game when it comes to drawing Taipei back to the mainland, political analysts said on Monday.

"For both Beijing and Taipei, Hong Kong will continue to be an indispensable intermediary in cross-straits relations," Chu Yun-han of National Taiwan University told a forum on Hong's Kong's transition to Chinese rule.
Hong Kong and Taiwan last week named high-level point men to improve channels of communication, but Beijing was quick to say no official contact could take place without its approval.

Hong Kong, which became China's newest and richest region on July 1 after 156 years of British rule, has earned its place in the Taiwan Straits triangle because of its location near both China and Taiwan as well as its economic might, Chu said.
China has viewed Taiwan as a rebel province since the former Chinese Nationalist government fled to the island after losing the civil war to the communists in 1949.

A smooth transition for Hong Kong is in the best interests of China, which is seeking Taiwan's reunification with the mainland under the same "one country, two systems" policy it used to recover the former British colony, said Cheng Tun-jen of Taiwan's Institute for National Policy Research.

By being "reasonable" with Hong Kong, he said, China can show the international community and notably the critical United States it has succeeded in putting two political and economic systems under one roof and call Taiwan unreasonable.
"The way to reunification is not through Hong Kong but through Washington," he said.
Hong Kong has benefited from the political and diplomatic acrimony stirred by the Beijing-Taipei conflict by acting as the conduit for business between the mainland and the island.
Despite a ban on direct commercial links, Taiwan has pumped up to US$30 billion into China, most of it via Hong Kong.

But Cheng says Taiwan has been losing its "economic leverage" because of the rise of democracy, a resurfacing of nationalism and the power of capitalism which compound an already tricky relationship between Beijing and Taipei.
"Both sides of the strait have been driven apart rather than coming together for quite a while," he said.
As Taiwan has pushed itself further onto the world stage, China has been promoting nationalism and experimenting with its own brand of capitalism, he said.
"Nationalism is a political hedge against economic downturn in the People's Republic of China," Cheng said.
Beijing test-fired missiles into the sea off Taiwan on the eve of the island's presidential elections in March 1996 and has vowed to attack if Taipei proclaims independence.
Chu said Taipei will get some breathing space as Beijing turns its energy to managing its new region and preparing for the Communist Party congress and a possible Sino-U.S. summit later this year.
"Hong Kong is not the place and 1997 is not the time for making a political score," he said.
